Describe a positive association between two numerical variables in words.



What is the difference between form and direction in a scatterplot description?



Two-way table: Robin Urban=8, Robin Rural=2 (row total=10). Sparrow Urban=4, Sparrow Rural=6 (row total=10). What is the row proportion of Sparrows that are Rural?



Using the same bird table (Urban total=12, Rural total=8). What is the column proportion of Urban birds that are Robin?



What is the difference between a joint proportion and a marginal proportion in a two-way table?



When would you prefer a 100% stacked bar (position = 'fill') over a regular stacked bar?


Click to reveal answers — Section C — Association description and two-way tables (Read 2)


As one variable increases, the other tends to increase as well (upward trend in the scatterplot).
Form is the shape of the trend (linear, curved, no pattern). Direction is whether higher \(x\) goes with higher \(y\) (positive), lower \(y\) (negative), or no consistent change (none).
\(6/10 = 0.60\) — 60% of Sparrows are in Rural habitat (denominator is Sparrow row total).
\(8/12 \approx 0.667\) — about 67% of Urban birds are Robins (denominator is Urban column total).
Joint: fraction of ALL observations in one specific cell (divide by grand total). Marginal: fraction in a row or column total (divide by grand total for that row or column).
When you want to compare proportions within groups rather than raw counts — especially when group sizes differ, so the bars all reach 100% and the composition is easier to compare.

text:

What is the main purpose of %>% (pipe) in the tidyverse?



Which tidyverse function keeps rows that satisfy a logical condition (e.g. weight > 50)?



Which function chooses columns by name?



Which function adds a new column while keeping the original number of rows?



Which function counts how many rows fall in each level of a categorical variable?



What is the role of group_by(species) before summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g))?



After group_by(island), you call summarize(n = n(), avg = mean(bill_length_mm)). What do you get?



Name two things glimpse(df) shows.


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Tidyverse pipeline verbs (Read 1 · pipeline)


The pipe passes the result of the left side as the first argument to the function on the right — it chains steps so you can read the pipeline top to bottom.
filter() — it returns only rows where the condition is TRUE.
select() — e.g. select(species, body_mass_g) returns a data frame with only those columns.
mutate() — e.g. mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) creates a new column.
count(variable) — returns a data frame with one row per level and a column n with the count.
group_by() splits the data by species so summarize() returns one summary row per species instead of one row for the whole dataset.
One row per island with two columns: n (count of penguins on that island) and avg (mean bill length for that island).
Variable names, types (e.g. <dbl>, <chr>), total rows and columns, and a short preview of values.









Classify each as numerical or categorical (and binary if categorical):

Penguin flipper length (mm)

Island: Biscoe / Dream / Torgersen

Sex: male/female

Clutch completion: yes/no

Bill depth (mm)




For one numerical variable, name one graph and two numeric summaries.



For one categorical variable, name one graph and one numeric summary.



Why might you report the median instead of the mean for a numerical variable?


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Variable types and one-variable summaries



Numerical. b) Categorical, not binary. c) Categorical, binary. d) Categorical, binary. e) Numerical.

Graph: histogram (or dot plot/boxplot). Numeric: mean + SD (symmetric) or median + IQR (skewed/outliers).
Graph: bar chart. Numeric: counts or proportions per category.
The median is resistant to outliers — extreme values pull the mean but not the median, so median better represents a ‘typical’ value when data are skewed or have outliers.









Data: \(4, 6, 8, 10, 10, 12, 14, 16\). Compute the range.



Dataset N: \(7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 13\). Find \(Q_1\), \(Q_3\), and IQR.



List the five numbers in the five-number summary in order.



Describe how a boxplot represents the five-number summary.



In words, what does the sample standard deviation \(s\) measure?



When would you prefer IQR over SD to describe spread? Why?


Click to reveal answers — Section C — Spread: range, IQR, and standard deviation


Range \(= \max - \min = 16 - 4 = 12\).
Lower half: \(7, 8, 9, 10\) → \(Q_1 = (8+9)/2 = 8.5\). Upper half: \(10, 11, 12, 13\) → \(Q_3 = (11+12)/2 = 11.5\). IQR \(= 3\).
Minimum, \(Q_1\) (first quartile), Median (\(Q_2\)), \(Q_3\) (third quartile), Maximum.
The box spans \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\); the line inside is the median; whiskers extend to the min and max (or fences if outliers are shown as dots).
\(s\) measures the typical distance of individual observations from their mean — a larger \(s\) means values are more spread out from \(\bar{x}\).
When the data are skewed or have outliers — IQR is based only on the middle 50% and is resistant to extremes, while SD uses all values and is sensitive to outliers.

title: Module 4 — Quiz B (Concept Check)
text:
Reading: Module 4 Read 2 (complete Read 1 + Quiz A first)
Canvas: Concept Check quiz (Module 4)
Apply design classification, methods-map matching, and R output reading from Read 1–2.
Full integration, simulation, and error scenarios → Synthesis.





60 volunteers randomly assigned to aerobic exercise or stretching for 8 weeks; resting heart rate measured.

RCT or observational? 2. Can we make a causal claim? 3. What is the confounder risk?




Survey of 200 adults; self-reported diet quality and cholesterol level compared.

RCT or observational? 2. Causal claim? 3. Confounder risk?




Schools randomly assigned to new or traditional math curriculum; end-of-year scores compared.

RCT or observational? 2. Unit of randomization? 3. Confounder risk?




Employees who drink ≥ 2 cups/day report higher productivity. Identify a likely confounder and explain the DAG path.


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Design classification (Read 1; revisit with R in mind)



RCT. 2. Yes — random assignment supports causation. 3. Low — randomization distributes confounders across groups.


Observational. 2. No — association only; diet is self-selected. 3. High — age, income, lifestyle are likely confounders.


RCT (cluster-randomized by school). 2. School (not individual student). 3. Low at school level — within-school confounders remain.

Example: sleep quality — people who sleep well drink more coffee AND report higher productivity. DAG: sleep → coffee (EV) and sleep → productivity (RV).









Two independent groups; outcome is blood pressure (numerical). Which test and R function?



Two groups; outcome is recovered (yes/no). Sample sizes \(n_1=80\), \(n_2=75\). Which test and R function?



Same students tested before and after an intervention. Which design — matched pairs or independent groups? Which test?



When using chisq.test(), what condition must you check?



Why does R’s t.test() use the Welch approximation by default (not equal-variance t)?


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Methods-map matching (Read 2 §1)


Welch two-sample t-test. R: t.test(bp ~ group, data = df). Conditions: independence, reasonably normal or large \(n\) per group.
Two-proportion z-test or chi-square test of independence. R: prop.test(c(x1, x2), c(80, 75)) or chisq.test(table(df$group, df$recovered)).
Matched pairs (same units, two measurements). Use a paired t-test on differences: t.test(df$post - df$pre) or t.test(post, pre, paired = TRUE).
All expected cell counts ≥ 5 (or ≥ 1 by relaxed rule). If violated, use Fisher’s exact test or combine categories.
Welch does not assume equal population variances across groups — more robust and appropriate unless you have strong evidence the variances are equal.









Welch two-sample t-test: \(p = 0.03\), 95% CI \([1.2, 8.6]\) (Group B \(-\) Group A). State the decision (\(\alpha=0.05\)) and interpret the CI.



Two-proportion z-test: \(p = 0.18\), 95% CI \([-0.02, 0.10]\) (proportion difference). State the decision (\(\alpha=0.05\)).



Two groups; \(H_0\): mean blood pressure is the same in both groups. Write the null and alternative hypotheses using \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\).


Click to reveal answers — Section C — Read two-group R output (Read 2 §1)


Reject \(H_0\) (p < 0.05). We are 95% confident the population mean for Group B exceeds Group A by between 1.2 and 8.6 units.
Fail to reject \(H_0\) (p > 0.05). Insufficient evidence of a difference in population proportions.
\(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) (or \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\)) vs \(H_a: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2\) (two-sided) or directed alternative if specified.

title: Module 4 — Quiz A (Def & Notation)
text:
Reading: Module 4 Read 1
Project: Project 4 · Canvas: Def & Notation quiz (Module 4)
Work these practice items after Read 1. Sections follow Read 1: study-design vocabulary (EV, RV, RCT, observational, confounder, DAG) and causal language.
Methods-map matching and R output → Quiz B after Read 2.





Define explanatory variable (EV) in one or two clear sentences.



Define response variable (RV) in one or two clear sentences.



Define observational study and distinguish it from a randomized experiment.



Define randomized controlled trial (RCT) and state its key feature.



Define confounder in one sentence. Give one example.



Draw or describe a DAG (directed acyclic graph) with one confounder \(C\) affecting both \(X\) (EV) and \(Y\) (RV).



State what a p-value does NOT establish for a two-group difference in an observational study.



Explain in one sentence why random assignment is the key tool for causal inference.


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Study-design vocabulary (Read 1 §1)


The explanatory variable is the variable that explains, predicts, or is thought to cause changes in the response — typically the treatment, exposure, or grouping factor.
The response variable is the outcome of interest — the variable we measure to see whether it changes with the explanatory variable.
An observational study records data on individuals as they are, without the researcher assigning treatments. Group membership is determined by the individuals themselves, not by random assignment.
An RCT is an experiment in which participants are randomly assigned to treatment or control groups by the researcher, so group membership is not self-selected.
A confounder is a variable associated with both the EV and RV that can create or distort the apparent association between them. Example: age is a confounder in a study of coffee and heart disease.
\(C \rightarrow X\) and \(C \rightarrow Y\). This ‘backdoor path’ from \(X\) to \(Y\) through \(C\) creates confounded association if \(C\) is not controlled.
A p-value does not establish causation. Even a very small p-value only indicates the difference is unlikely under \(H_0\); confounders can still explain an observational association.
Random assignment distributes known and unknown confounders approximately equally across groups on average, so observed group differences are attributable to the treatment.









Classify each claim: causal (requires RCT) or association only (observational):

“Students who took the tutoring program scored higher on the exam.”
“Students randomly assigned to tutoring scored higher on the exam.”




A measured confounder exists in an observational study. What technique can partially account for it, and what is its limitation?



Study: older employees have higher salaries and are more likely to be managers. Is “age” a confounder for the association between managerial status and salary? Explain.


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Causal language vs association language (Read 1 §1–2)



Association only — students self-selected into tutoring; confounders likely. b) Causal — random assignment supports the tutoring → higher score claim.

Subclassification / stratification: compare groups within levels of the confounder. Limitation: only controls for measured confounders; unmeasured confounders remain.
Yes. Age is associated with both being a manager (EV) and salary (RV), so it can create or distort the managerial status → salary association.

title: Module 4 — Synthesis Quiz
text:
Readings: Read 0, Read 1, Read 2
Labs: Demo, Exercise
Canvas: Synthesis quiz (Module 4) · two attempts, highest score counts
Full integration for Project 4: interpret two-group CIs, connect study design to causal language, read t.test() / prop.test() output, simulation workflow, and four lab situations (numerical vs binary outcome; validate against known truth).




Open notes (methods map, R reference).
Use the CI interpretation template from Read 2: “I am 95% confident that…”
For R items, match the workflow in the demo lab and your Project 4 templates.





Use: “I am 95% confident that [population parameter difference] is between [L] and [U]. In this context, confidence means that if data from many samples were collected the same way, then 95% of the intervals computed would contain the true difference.”


RCT; 95% CI for mean sleep change (treatment \(-\) control): [0.4, 1.8] hours. Interpret in context.



95% CI for difference in recovery proportions (new \(-\) standard treatment): [0.05, 0.22]. Interpret.



95% CI for mean score difference (tutoring \(-\) control): [$-$2.1, 8.4]. Interpret. What does zero in the interval mean?



Which is the best interpretation of a 95% CI for a mean difference?

95% probability the difference is in this specific interval.
Repeated sampling: ~95% of such intervals contain the true parameter.
95% of individuals differ by this amount.



Click to reveal answers — Section A — Interpret two-group confidence intervals


I am 95% confident the true mean increase in sleep for the treatment group compared to control is between 0.4 and 1.8 hours (with confidence-level sentence).
I am 95% confident the true difference in recovery proportions (new minus standard) is between 0.05 and 0.22 — the new treatment has a higher recovery rate in the population.
Zero is a plausible value → we cannot conclude a nonzero population difference at the 95% level. We are 95% confident the difference is between $-$2.1 and 8.4 points.
B is correct. A treats the parameter as random after data are observed; C confuses parameter with individual observations.









RCT: 120 volunteers randomly assigned to two diets; weight loss compared after 12 weeks. p = 0.01. Write a valid causal conclusion.



Observational: employees who use standing desks report 15% higher productivity. p = 0.04. Write a valid (non-causal) conclusion.



A news headline reads: “Coffee causes longer life — study of 50,000 adults.” The study was observational. What is wrong with the headline?



Name one situation where an RCT is impossible or unethical and explain why observational methods are used instead.


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Study-design integration (causal vs association)


Valid: Random assignment supports a causal interpretation — the low-carb diet caused greater weight loss on average (p = 0.01), ruling out confounding by baseline differences.
Valid (association-only): Employees who use standing desks are associated with higher productivity (p = 0.04), but unmeasured confounders (e.g. health motivation) could explain the difference.
The study is observational — causation cannot be established because coffee drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in unmeasured ways (e.g. diet, socioeconomic status). The headline overstates the design’s conclusions.
Examples: studying the effect of smoking on lung cancer (cannot assign people to smoke); natural disasters on mental health; childhood poverty on outcomes. Observational methods are used because random assignment is unethical or infeasible.







These R patterns support the simulation and analysis in the demo lab and Project 4.


What does set.seed(123) do and why is it used in simulation?



Write a tidyverse pipeline that computes mean and SD of outcome for each level of group in df.



Write a ggplot2 call for a boxplot of outcome by group in df.



Which R call runs a Welch two-sample t-test of outcome by group in df?



Two groups: group A has \(x_1 = 30\) successes in \(n_1 = 80\); group B has \(x_2 = 45\) in \(n_2 = 90\). Write the prop.test call.



Write ggplot2 code for a 100% stacked bar comparing binary outcome proportions across two groups.


Click to reveal answers — Section C — R workflow for two-group comparison (Read 2 · Lab)


Fixes the random number generator state so that simulation results are reproducible — running the script again gives the same random draws.
df %>% group_by(group) %>% summarize(mean = mean(outcome), sd = sd(outcome))
ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = outcome)) + geom_boxplot()
t.test(outcome ~ group, data = df) — formula interface; Welch is the default (var.equal = FALSE).
prop.test(c(30, 45), c(80, 90))
ggplot(df, aes(x = group, fill = outcome)) + geom_bar(position = 'fill') + labs(y = 'Proportion')









Test if a new drug reduces symptoms more than placebo (\(H_a: \mu_{\text{drug}} < \mu_{\text{placebo}}\)). State Type I and Type II errors in context.



Test if a training program improves pass rates (\(H_a: p_{\text{trained}} > p_{\text{control}}\)). State errors in context.



Welch t-test; \(p = 0.08\); \(\alpha = 0.05\). Which decision? Which error type is now possible?



Two-proportion z-test; \(p = 0.003\); \(\alpha = 0.05\). Decision? Which error type is possible?


Click to reveal answers — Section D — Error types in two-group design context


Type I: conclude drug is better when it is not (approve ineffective drug). Type II: fail to detect that the drug works (miss effective treatment).
Type I: conclude training helps when it does not. Type II: miss a beneficial training program.
Fail to reject \(H_0\). Type II error is now possible — we might be missing a real difference.
Reject \(H_0\). Type I error is possible — we might be incorrectly concluding the proportions differ.







Match each scenario to the correct test and simulation plan. See the demo lab Problems 1–4.


Binary EV (treatment vs control), numerical RV (e.g. recovery days). \(n_1 = 30\), \(n_2 = 30\), true \(\mu_1 = 10\), \(\mu_2 = 12\).
Which simulation approach and which test?



Binary EV, binary RV (success/fail). \(n_1 = 50\), \(n_2 = 50\), true \(p_1 = 0.4\), \(p_2 = 0.6\).
Simulation and test?



After simulating with a known true difference, how do you validate that your code is correct?



Simulated RCT with random assignment: p = 0.02 for group difference. Write the conclusion connecting the design to causation.


Click to reveal answers — Section E — Demo lab: simulation + two-group test situations


Simulate with rnorm(30, mean = 10) and rnorm(30, mean = 12). Test: Welch two-sample t-test (t.test(days ~ group)).
Simulate with rbinom(50, 1, 0.4) and rbinom(50, 1, 0.6). Test: two-proportion z-test (prop.test(c(x1, x2), c(50, 50))).
Run many simulations (e.g. 1000 reps); check that the estimated rejection rate near the true effect matches expected power, and that the CI covers the true parameter ~95% of the time.
Because of random assignment, the group difference is attributable to the simulated treatment, not confounding. We reject \(H_0\) (p = 0.02) and conclude the treatment caused the observed difference in the simulation.

title: Module 5 — Quiz B (Concept Check)
text:
Reading: Module 5 Read 2 (complete Read 1 + Quiz A first)
Canvas: Concept Check quiz (Module 5)
Apply residual conditions for inference, interpret CIs for slope, and distinguish CI for mean response from prediction interval.
Full regression workflow, R output, and lab situations → Synthesis.





What assumption about residuals supports confidence and prediction intervals in regression?



Name two visual checks used to assess residual normality in regression.



If a residual plot shows a clear funnel shape (spread increases with \(x\)), what concern does this raise?


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Residual conditions for inference (Read 2 §1)


Residuals should be approximately normally distributed with constant spread (homoscedasticity) across all values of \(x\).

We are 95% confident the mean exam score among all students who study 10 hours is between 76.1 and 80.5 points.

title: Module 5 — Quiz A (Def & Notation)
text:
Reading: Module 5 Read 1
Project: Project 5 · Canvas: Def & Notation quiz (Module 5)
Work these practice items after Read 1. Sections follow Read 1: scatterplot vocabulary, regression line notation (slope, intercept, prediction), and residuals / MSE / R².
Inference for slope, CI vs PI → Quiz B after Read 2.





Define form in the context of describing a scatterplot.



Define direction in the context of a scatterplot.



Define strength in the context of a scatterplot.



Define Pearson correlation \(r\) and state its range.



What does the sign of \(r\) tell you? What does \(|r|\) close to 1 vs close to 0 tell you?


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Scatterplot vocabulary (Read 1 §1)


Form describes the overall shape of the pattern — whether the relationship looks roughly linear, curved, or neither (no pattern).
Direction is positive (both variables tend to increase together), negative (one increases as the other decreases), or none (no consistent direction).
Strength describes how closely the points cluster around a trend — strong (tight cluster), moderate, weak, or none.
Pearson \(r\) is a unitless measure of the strength and direction of a linear association between two numerical variables; it ranges from \(-1\) to \(1\).
\(r > 0\): positive direction (as \(x\) increases, \(y\) tends to increase). \(r < 0\): negative. \(|r|\) near 1: strong linear association. \(|r|\) near 0: weak to no linear association.









Write the simple linear regression prediction equation and identify each symbol.



State the general interpretation template for a slope \(b_1\) in context.



State the general interpretation template for the intercept \(b_0\).



Exam-score model: \(\hat{y} = 47.7 + 3.06x\) (study hours). Predict the score for a student studying 8 hours.



Write the R call to fit a simple linear regression of height_cm on dose using a data frame plant_dat.


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Regression line notation (Read 1 §1)


\(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\). \(\hat{y}\): predicted (fitted) value of the response. \(b_0\): intercept (predicted \(y\) when \(x=0\)). \(b_1\): slope (predicted change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\)). \(x\): value of the explanatory variable.
For each additional one-unit increase in \(x\), the predicted value of \(y\) changes by \(b_1\) units (increases if \(b_1>0\), decreases if \(b_1<0\)).
The intercept \(b_0\) is the predicted value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\). Caution: this is only meaningful if \(x = 0\) is a plausible value in context.
\(\hat{y} = 47.7 + 3.06(8) = 47.7 + 24.48 = 72.18\) points.
lm(height_cm ~ dose, data = plant_dat) (or assign to an object: fit <- lm(height_cm ~ dose, data = plant_dat)).









Define a residual for an observation \((x_i, y_i)\) with fitted value \(\hat{y}_i\).



What does the least-squares method minimize to choose the best regression line?



Define test MSE and explain why it is preferred over training MSE for evaluating a model.



Interpret \(R^2 = 0.68\) on the test set for a study-hours → exam-score model.


Click to reveal answers — Section C — Residuals, MSE, and R² (Read 1 §1)


Residual \(= y_i - \hat{y}_i\) — the difference between the observed response and the model’s predicted response.
Least-squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals \(\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\) — no other line produces a smaller total.
Test MSE \(= \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\) on held-out data. It is preferred because training MSE is optimistically biased — the model was fit on those same points, so training MSE understates error on new data.
The linear model explains about 68% of the variability in exam scores in the test set. The remaining 32% is unexplained by study hours alone.

title: Module 5 — Synthesis Quiz
text:
Readings: Read 0, Read 1, Read 2
Labs: Demo, Exercise
Canvas: Synthesis quiz (Module 5) · two attempts, highest score counts
Full integration for Project 5: read scatterplots, interpret \(r\), interpret regression output, predict with predict(), distinguish CI vs PI, and reflect on the five-project portfolio.




Open notes (methods map, R reference).
Use the interpretation templates from Read 1–2.
For R items, match the workflow in the demo lab.







A scatterplot shows fertilizer dose (x) and plant height in cm (y): the points slope upward and cluster tightly near a line. Describe the association using form, direction, and strength.



A scatterplot of age and reading speed shows a clear arc (reading peaks in mid-life and declines at both ends). Is Pearson correlation an appropriate summary? Explain.


Click to reveal answers — Section A — Reading a scatterplot


Form: roughly linear. Direction: positive (more fertilizer → taller plant). Strength: strong (points cluster tightly).
No — Pearson \(r\) measures linear association only. A curved (non-linear) form makes \(r\) a misleading summary of the relationship.









R gives cor(exercise_min, resting_hr) = −0.78. Interpret this value in context.



R output: (Intercept) 79.1, exercise_min −0.30. Write the fitted equation and interpret the slope.



Using the equation above, predict resting HR for someone who exercises 30 min/day.



A person exercises 30 min/day and has a resting HR of 74 bpm. Using the model above, compute their residual.


Click to reveal answers — Section B — Interpreting correlation and regression output


Strong negative linear association: as daily exercise minutes increase, resting heart rate tends to decrease. The relationship is strong (\(|r|\) close to 1).
\(\hat{\text{resting HR}} = 79.1 - 0.30\,(\text{exercise min})\). Slope: each additional minute of daily exercise is associated with a predicted 0.30 bpm decrease in resting heart rate.
\(\hat{y} = 79.1 - 0.30(30) = 79.1 - 9.0 = 70.1\) bpm.
Residual \(= 74 - 70.1 = 3.9\) bpm — they have a resting HR 3.9 bpm higher than the model predicts.









For the plant model, confint(fit_plant, 'dose') → [1.7, 2.6]. Interpret in context.



The 95% CI for slope is \([0.001, 0.003]\), not containing 0. Is this association statistically significant? Is it practically significant?


Click to reveal answers — Section C — CI for slope


We are 95% confident that each additional unit of fertilizer dose changes the mean plant height by between 1.7 and 2.6 cm.
Statistically significant (CI excludes 0). Practical significance depends on context — a change of 0.001–0.003 units per 1-unit increase may be too small to matter in practice.









A biologist wants to estimate the average plant height for all plants given exactly 7 units of fertilizer. Should they use interval = 'confidence' or interval = 'prediction'?



A researcher wants an interval for one specific new plant given 7 units of fertilizer. Which interval?



At \(x_0 = 7\): CI for mean = \([22.8, 25.6]\); PI for individual = \([13.1, 35.3]\). What accounts for the large difference in width?


Click to reveal answers — Section D — Mean-response CI vs prediction interval


interval = 'confidence' — this estimates where the mean response (average outcome) falls, not an individual plant.
interval = 'prediction' — this covers where one individual future observation is likely to fall.
The PI adds individual-to-individual variability on top of uncertainty in the mean. Even if we knew the mean exactly, individual plants would vary widely around it.









Write the R commands (in order) to: (1) fit a regression of weight_g on length_cm using stones_dat, (2) extract the slope CI, (3) predict with a 95% PI at length_cm = 15.



After summary(fit), you see Estimate for length_cm is 12.4 with Std. Error 1.8 and Pr(>|t|) = 0.0003. What do these tell you?



Your team collected stone weights (g) and widths (cm) in a shared Google Sheet. List the steps to get this data into R and fit a regression.


Click to reveal answers — Section E — Lab situations: Project 5 workflow


```r fit <- lm(weight_g ~ length_cm, data = stones_dat) confint(fit, ‘length_cm’) predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(length_cm = 15), interval = ‘prediction’)


2. Slope estimate: 12.4 g per cm. The test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ rejects at $p=0.0003$ — strong evidence of a linear association. The SE of 1.8 reflects uncertainty in the slope estimate.

3. 1. Export sheet as CSV. 2. `dat <- read_csv('stones.csv')` (or use the URL). 3. Check `head(dat)`. 4. `fit <- lm(weight_g ~ width_cm, data = dat)`. 5. `summary(fit)` to read slope and intercept.

</details>
:::

title: Course Path
text:
This page shows the recommended path through the course during the five-week summer session from June 1 to July 2, 2026. You may work at your own pace within each module window, but the modules should be done in the order shown. Check Canvas to turn in work, take quizzes, see grades, and join discussions.
Each project module follows the same pattern: Read 0 (project preview) → read → update your reference sheets → low-stakes quizzes (as many times as you want) → lab (Wednesday) → synthesis quiz (Thursday) → project milestone (Friday) → project (Sunday). Module 5 is shorter and ends on Thursday, July 2.
Reference sheets (methods map, R reference) grow a little in every module 1–5. All readings also live on the lectures index if you want the full list.
Outcomes below are tagged essential (needed for the module project or core module goals) or optional (helpful enrichment or stretch).

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Cal Poly Humboldt — Spring 2026



Course Number: STAT 109
Course Title: Introductory Biostatistics
Units: 4
Semester: Spring 2026
Mode of Instruction: In-person
General Education: Lower Division GE Area B4 – Mathematical Concepts & Quantitative Reasoning


Days/Time: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 11:00–11:50 AM
Location: BSS 166



9:00–10:50 AM, LOCATION: FH 202
11:00–12:50 PM, LOCATION: FH 202
1:00–2:50 PM, LOCATION: FH 202



Optional Final Exam (held during the scheduled final exam period): Wednesday, May 13, 2026, 10:20–12:10 PM, BSS 166.The final exam is optional and may be taken to replace a midterm grade.



Teacher: Dr. Rosanna Overholser
Email: rho3@humboldt.edu
Office Location: BSS 334
Office Phone: 707-826-4022
Office Hours: Mondays 2-3pm, Wednesdays 12-12:50pm, and Fridays 10-10:50am or by appointment
Please use your Cal Poly Humboldt email account to contact me and check both Canvas and your Cal Poly Humboldt email regularly for course communications.





Descriptive statistics, probability, random variables, discrete and continuous distributions, confidence intervals, contingency tests, regression and correlation, tests of hypothesis, analysis of variance. Emphasis: methods and applications used in the biological and natural resource sciences.
Division: Lower Division  Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs. Activity 2 hrs.  Instruction Mode: In-person
Prerequisite: MATH 101 or MATH 101I or MATH 102 or MATH 109B (may be taken concurrently with instructor approval) with a grade of C- or better or ALEKS PPL assessment score over 65 or appropriate high school coursework. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details. MATH 102 may be taken concurrently with instructor approval.
Note: if you plan to use STAT 109 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA or STAT course, you must have a grade of C- or better in this course.


By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Use numerical and graphical descriptive statistics to summarize and interpret data.
Explain the role of randomness, probability, and sampling in statistical inference.
Apply probability rules and work with common probability distributions.
Construct and interpret confidence intervals for means and proportions.
Conduct and interpret basic hypothesis tests.
Analyze relationships between pairs of variables using correlation and regression.
Use a statistical programming language to analyze data and communicate results.
Distinguish between correlation and causation and recognize limitations of statistical conclusions.




This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Quantitative Reasoning) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.





STAT 109 includes:

Three weekly lecture meetings
One weekly laboratory session

In this 4-unit course, students should expect to spend approximately 12 hours per week on course-related work, including time in lecture (3 hours), lab time (2 hours), and time outside of class to do practice problems, projects and prepare for exams and quizzes (7 hours).


Lecture Notes: I’ll provide packets of guided notes to you in class. These notes have key concepts, definitions and word problems that we’ll solve during class time. These notes have spaces for you to fill in during lecture as we go. If you need to miss class, please ask me for the packet you will be missing.
Optional Textbook: Introductory Statistics for the Life and Biomedical Sciences by Julie Vu and Dave Harrington, available for free online.
Three Binder: Please bring a three-ring binder to class to keep the lecture note packets in.
Pen or Pencil: Please bring a pen or pencil to class to take notes with.
Software: R (free and installed on all campus computers; see R download page to install on your own computer) 
Calculator: Scientific (not graphing) calculator 
Other Technology: Regular access to a computer with reliable internet



Students who do not have personal access to required technology may use campus computer labs and library resources. If you want to get a free used computer, please check to see if our campus’s Reuseable Office Supply Exchange (ROSE) has one available.



There are no additional course fees beyond standard tuition and registration fees.






Students will complete a variety of assessments:

Daily warm-up problems (Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, in lecture)
Weekly programming labs (due Tuesdays, in Canvas: I’ll help you write the code the Thursday before)
Weekly quizzes based on practice problems and labs (Thursdays at the beginning of lab)
Two midterms (Week 6 and Week 13 Fridays, in lecture)
Five projects (due on assigned dates in Canvas; see important dates below)

Daily warm-up problems are designed to give you an opportunity to work as a team with your classmates. Weekly labs and quizzes are designed to provide regular formative feedback through practice problems, posted solutions, and in-lab support. Midterms require students to demonstrate their understanding of the course material. Projects allow students to apply their knowledge to practical, real-world problems and can be used as part of a portfolio.
Optionally, students may take a final exam (held during the scheduled final exam period: Wednesday, May 13, 2026, 10:20–12:10 PM, BSS 166) to replace a midterm grade.






Component
Weight




Daily Participation
5%


Weekly quizzes
30%


Weekly labs
15%


Two midterms
30%


Five projects
20%


Total
100%



Final letter grades will be assigned based on overall performance according to the following:
A: 93-100% A-: 90-92% B+: 87-89% B: 83-86% B-: 80-82% C+: 77-79% C: 73-76% C-: 70-72% D: 60-69% F: 0-59%
Note:

Grade Mode: Letter grade by default. Students may elect Credit/No Credit grading according to university deadlines and procedures.
A minimum grade of C- is required for the course to count toward GE Area B4.
If you stop attending class and stop doing assignments without communicating with me, you will receive a grade of WU (Withdrawal Unsatisfactory). Please communicate with me early if you are having difficulties: it’s possible that I can help you get back on track, or help you obtain a more appropriate grade (W or I) for your situation.




Regular attendance and active participation are expected and essential for success in this course.

Attendance in lecture will be tracked via participation in the warm-up problems.
Attendance in lab will be tracked via participation in the quizzes.

If you must miss class, you are responsible for obtaining notes and keeping up with course material.





The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Daily attendance in lecture is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 days of lecture without penalty and without contacting me. It’s up to you to reserve these days for emergencies only. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss lecture or are absent for more than two weeks so if you find yourself in this situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution to getting back on track.
Weekly quizzes during Thursday lab sessions are required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss lab due to illness or other emergencies. If this happens, please contact me to make an arrangement to take the quiz at another time.
Weekly programming labs are due Tuesdays in Canvas. After the due date, a solution will be posted, so late submissions are generally not accepted except in documented emergencies. These labs will be graded on completion and your reflection.
Projects are due on the specified date in Canvas. You may submit a late project up to a week late with no penalty. After a week, a project can be turn in for 70% of the grade.
Midterms are required. If you need to miss a midterm due to illness or other emergencies, please communicate with me as soon as possible to reschedule it. Alternatively, you may take the optional final exam (Wednesday, May 13, 2026, 10:20–12:10 PM, BSS 166) to replace a missed midterm grade.

Note: Technology issues (internet access, device failure, software problems) are not automatically considered valid excuses for late or missed work; students are expected to plan accordingly.



Much of your course grade will be based on materials that you produce in-class without having AI as a resource. But you may use AI, such as NotebookLM or ChatGPT, in this course to help you learn the materials or to perform data analyses or on the projects.
For work that you do at home that is turned in for a grade I have two requirements:

if you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).

Be responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of all (AI assisted or not) materials you turn in.

I may use AI to assist me in my delivery of the course material, such as asking AI to see if an assignment is appropriate for a college level course or if the wording of a quiz question could be improved. I will not use AI to grade your work or use an AI detection tool to check your work.

if you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).

# Module 0 — baby-matching simulation (pattern)
set.seed(109)
mothers <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
num_correct <- numeric(10000)
for (i in 1:10000) {
  babies <- sample(c(1, 2, 3, 4))
  num_correct[i] <- sum(babies == mothers)
}
mean(num_correct == 4)   # P(all 4 correct)
mean(num_correct == 0)   # P(none correct)

# Module 0 — baby-matching simulation (pattern)
set.seed(109)
mothers <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)

  babies <- sample(c(1, 2, 3, 4))
  num_correct[i] <- sum(babies == mothers)

mean(num_correct == 4)   # P(all 4 correct)

title: Resources
text:
This page provides links to essential course resources including the textbook, R software downloads, and reference materials.


Lectures - Access all course lectures organized by week and day.



Optional Textbook: Introductory Statistics for the Life and Biomedical Sciences by Julie Vu and Dave Harrington
This textbook is available for free online and provides additional explanations and examples that complement the course materials.



STAT 109 uses R for statistical computing. You can use R in several ways:


Download R: R Project Website
R is free and open-source statistical software. The base R installation includes the core R language and basic packages.

Windows: Download the installer from CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network)
Mac: Download the macOS installer from CRAN
Linux: Install via your distribution’s package manager or from CRAN




Download RStudio: RStudio Desktop
RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R that provides a user-friendly interface, code editor, and helpful features for data analysis. RStudio Desktop is free and works with base R.
Note: You must install base R first before installing RStudio.



Access R in Google Colab: R in Colab
Google Colab provides free access to R in a cloud-based notebook environment. This is useful if you don’t want to install R on your computer or need to work from different devices.



Install R for Jupyter: IRkernel Documentation
Jupyter Notebook is another notebook environment that supports R. To use R in Jupyter:

Install base R first
Install Jupyter Notebook or JupyterLab
Install the IRkernel package in R
Register the kernel with Jupyter

Note: R is also installed on all campus computers, so you can use the computer labs if you prefer not to install software on your personal computer.






R Quick Reference — tidyverse patterns (import, group_by, ggplot2, two-sample tests) and a Project 4 verification checklist.

ROSE (Reusable Office Supply Exchange): Free used computers may be available if you need a computer
